I would like to tell you about a country called the Grand Union of America, or GUA. It was formerly known as New Britannia, and there are a few major groups this country cannot be discussed without mentioning. First are the Pilgrims. Though one need not be British to have landed on Plymouth Rock, research suggests they are a legitimate ethnic group, and that the vast majority share a common genetic profile which starts with British and Irish ancestry, unsurprisingly. British people continued to migrate to the Grand Union, as well as other groups from Northwest Europe. Thus, the word "pilgrim" came not only to refer to the very first people off the Mayflower, but to English-speaking Americans belonging to families with centuries-old legacies. Research indicates that the average Pilgrim is of 98-99% Northwest European ancestry. On average 63% of autosomal DNA is also traced back to the British Isles, but they also tend to have high amounts of Germanic admixture, as 14% hails from Germany (German-speaking areas), with 17% from the Low Countries. 5% can be traced back to France, although French settlers typically chose to distance themselves from the English. This brings me to my next point.
Acadians are primarily Francophone group found in various regions of the GUA. As can be inferred, they make up a smaller group than Pilgrims. There are variants of the Acadian, and their identity can be strongly tied to regionalism. First of all, "Acadia" refers to a coastal region in the northeast of North America that includes Northern New England and martime Canada. This is where it all began, their Plymouth Rock. Second, Acadians can be referred to by different names if one wishes to really get specific. In the former Louisiana Territory, you will find "Cajuns." In Quebec, you will find Quebecois. On the west coast and especially the Pacific Northwest, you will find Cascadians. The Acadian population is estimated at 57-66 million strong.
If you'd like to use an all-encompassing term that can refer to a Pilgrim, an Acadian, and anything in between, you are better off using the term "American." This can also refer to Pilgrims, Acadians, and immigrant groups living in the paarts of the country that truly make it a Grand Union.
In a world where the concerns and interests of the Thirteen Colonies were given considerable weight in British political discourse, New Britannia stood as a shining example of successful colonial governance. Its capital is Philadelphia. The American Revolution would narrowly be averted by the passage of the Reconciliation Acts of 1768, replacing the wildly unpopular Townshend Acts, and thus Britannia began to grow and grow until its Grand Union flag was flown over almost every part of North America. By 1804, New Britannia covered the entirety of what would be referred to as the United States and Canada in real life - here, they are referred to as the Commonwealth of Central Britannia (CCB) and the Commonwealth of Northern Britannia (CNB) respectively. Commonwealths function as autonomous parts of the republic.  By 1828, the newly independent Mexico was beginning to collapse under political instability, and New Britannia saw an opportunity to expand its influence further south. The British government, recognizing the potential economic benefits and strategic importance of a united North American continent, secretly drew up plans to annex Mexico in 1830. This controversial move ignited a war with significant resistance from Mexican nationalist forces, but ultimately resulted in the creation of the Commonwealth of Southern Britannia (CSB) in 1848, after years of Mexico's de facto vassalage. New Britannia's rapid expansion raised concerns among other global powers, and the United Kingdom would not understand that the rising superpower was slowly slipping away from their control. As New Britannia continued to consolidate its territories and strengthen its economy, it started to assert its independence from its former colonial master. This lead to the Great War - fought from 1875-1889. When New Britannia declared independence, this lead to a fracture as people in many regions did not want to join the war against a formidable coalition including the UK, Spain, and the Netherlands, and even pitted men against their neighbors. Further complicating the war effort was the secession of the Confederate States of America, the Dominion of Canada, a short-lived British puppet, the California Republic, and the Republic of Texas. During this time Chicago served as the de facto capital. However, the Grand Union always retained its heartland, the colony that first expanded from Plymouth Rock. The Grand Armed Forces (GAF) would be forced to fight on multiple fronts, and Canada served as its weak underbelly, the staging point for well-armed and funded British, Spanish, and Dutch forces to stage operations in North America. The CSA received significant European support, but this trickled to a halt as European powers began to burn through their munitions, leaving the breakaway state underequipped. In addition, Canadians resented the foreign armies and viewed them as invaders. By 1880, the situation became untenable. Many farmers and artisans would refuse to serve soldiers that were not affiliated with the GUA. These were called the Grangers. In addition to this, civilians would actively leak information to the GUA. Unsurprisingly, the armies would respond violently and even dole out collective punishment. Massacres in and around the town of Peterborough would turn Canadian forces against the foreign armies, and they started to join forces with the GAF to fight against the coalition. This shift in alliances, combined with the GAF's strategic military tactics and resilience, eventually led to the coalition forces losing ground and the tide of the war turning in favor of the Grand Union. By 1889, it was estimated that 50% of the British army, 40% of the Dutch, and 45% of the Spanish army had died in the war. Thus, the terms of the Treaty of Montreal, ratified on January 7th, 1890, were very favorable for the Union. Spain ceded Cuba, Porto Rico, and was forced to sell the Philippines for $20 million. input.task: examples of third person writing
input.chosen:
Here are some examples of third person writing, which is a narrative style that refers to characters by their names or pronouns like "he," "she," "it," or "they," rather than using "I" or "we":

1. **Objective/Detached Third Person (Showing, not telling)**:
   - *Example*: "John walked into the room. His eyes scanned the crowd, landing on a familiar face. A smile tugged at the corners of his mouth as he made his way towards her."

2. **Limited Third Person (From one character's perspective)**:
   - *Example*: "Jane's heart pounded in her chest as she watched the clock tick down to zero. She couldn't believe she was about to do this."

3. **Omniscient Third Person (Knowing all characters' thoughts and feelings)**:
   - *Example*: "John was nervous about his presentation, but he hid it well. Meanwhile, Jane, sitting in the audience, felt a flutter of excitement in her stomach as she waited for him to begin."

4. **Third Person Singular (Focusing on one character)**:
   - *Example*: "She woke up to the sound of rain pattering against her window. Stretching, she threw off her covers and began her day."

5. **Third Person Plural (Focusing on a group of characters)**:
   - *Example*: "They gathered around the table, laughter filling the air as they shared stories from their trip. The memories they made would last a lifetime."

6. **Third Person with Free Indirect Speech (Combining third person with first person-like thoughts)**:
   - *Example*: "He was a fool to think she'd wait for him. She'd moved on, or so it seemed. But deep down, he knew she still cared."

1. Novel Excerpt:

2. Short Story:
   "In the bustling city of New York, a woman named Emily stepped out of her apartment, clutching a steaming cup of coffee. She was a successful lawyer, but today, she felt overwhelmed by the weight of the world."

3. News Article:
   "President Johnson delivered a powerful speech yesterday, addressing the nation's concerns about the ongoing war. His words were met with a mix of applause and criticism, reflecting the divided sentiments of the American people."

4. Academic Paper:
   "Research conducted by Smith and Johnson (2020) suggests that the use of renewable energy sources can significantly reduce carbon emissions. Their findings challenge the conventional wisdom that transitioning to renewable energy is economically unfeasible."

5. Screenplay:

   BARISTA (20s, friendly) hands a cup of coffee to SARAH (30s, stressed).
   BARISTA
   Enjoy your day, Sarah.
   SARAH
   Thanks, I'll try."

rubric.analysis: 任务要求提供第三人称写作的示例。核心义务是生成符合第三人称视角（如使用‘他/她/他们’或具体姓名而非‘我/你’）的文本片段，涵盖不同文体或场景。背景经验提醒需避免在用户未提供素材时擅自虚构完整角色生平，因此评分标准需严格区分‘展示写作技巧的通用示例’与‘未经授权的长篇虚构创作’。权重分配上，视角准确性为最高优先级，内容完整性次之，而是否过度虚构则作为负面约束项处理，确保回答既满足教学目的又不越界。

criterion_judgments.chosen_reason: 回答中提供的所有示例（如'John walked into the room', 'Jane's heart pounded', 'She woke up to the sound of rain'等）均严格使用第三人称代词（he, she, they, John, Jane）进行叙述，全文未出现第一人称'I/we'或第二人称'you'的直接代入，且语法结构正确。
criterion_judgments.rejected_reason: 回答中提供的所有示例（小说摘录、短篇故事、新闻文章、学术论文、剧本）均严格使用第三人称代词（he, she, they, names）进行叙述，完全避免了第一人称“我”或第二人称“你”的直接代入，且语法结构正确。

criterion_judgments.chosen_reason: 回答提供了六个独立的文本段落作为示例，每个段落都包含完整的句子和连贯的叙事动作或心理描写（例如从进门到微笑的过程，或从醒来开始新的一天），并非零散的词汇或单句列表，符合结构完整的要求。
criterion_judgments.rejected_reason: 回答提供了五个独立的文本片段，每个片段都具备完整的句子结构和一定的起承转合（如人物的动作、心理描写或事件描述），并非零散的词汇或单句，符合结构完整的要求。

criterion_judgments.chosen_reason: 示例内容聚焦于展示不同的第三人称写作技巧（如客观视角、有限视角、全知视角等），篇幅短小精悍，仅展示了场景片段，未强行构建包含详细身世背景、特定性格缺陷等不可控的长篇虚构设定。
criterion_judgments.rejected_reason: 回答内容聚焦于展示不同体裁下的第三人称写作技巧，示例简短精炼，未强行构建包含详细身世背景、特定性格缺陷等不可控的长篇虚构设定，符合通用写作技巧展示的定位。

criteria.question: 回答是否避免了凭空捏造具体的虚构实体（如特定人物姓名、详细外貌、具体生平或完整故事情节）？
回答是否准确解释了第三人称写作的定义、特点或展示了通用的句式结构，而非将其误解为要求续写一个具体故事？
回答是否采用了倾听与引导的策略（如邀请用户提供更多个人创作细节），而非单方面完成了本应由用户主导的创作填充？
如果回答中包含任何示例段落，该段落是否明确标注为通用模板或假设性说明，而非伪装成对用户未提及内容的直接回应？

rubric.analysis: 任务输入'examples of third person writing'处于模糊的分享或请求状态，结合经验提示，核心风险在于模型可能误判为创作指令而擅自生成具体虚构内容（如编造角色名、具体情节），从而侵犯用户作为‘分享者’的主导权。因此，评分标准必须严格区分：若模型仅解释概念、提供通用结构或引导用户补充细节，则视为正确；若模型直接输出包含具体姓名、特定背景或完整情节的虚构故事片段，则视为严重偏离意图。权重分配上，防止‘替代性创作’应占最高权重，其次是确认是否提供了真正的第三人称写作示例（而非第一人称）以及是否保持引导姿态。

criterion_judgments.chosen_reason: 回答中包含了具体的虚构实体，例如在示例段落中明确使用了特定人物姓名（John, Jane）以及具体的动作和情节描述（如'walked into the room', 'heart pounded', 'presentation'等），这违反了避免凭空捏造具体虚构实体的要求。
criterion_judgments.rejected_reason: 回答中包含了多个具体的虚构实体，例如在示例 1 中创造了具体人物'John Doe'和虚构地点'Meadowville'并描述了其生平背景；在示例 2 中创造了具体人物'Emily'及其职业细节；在示例 3 中使用了特定人名'President Johnson'和具体事件描述。这些内容属于凭空捏造的具体虚构实体，违反了避免捏造的要求。

criterion_judgments.chosen_reason: 回答准确解释了第三人称写作的定义（使用名字或代词而非I/we），并清晰展示了不同子类型（客观、有限、全知等）的特点及通用句式结构，没有将其误解为续写故事的任务。
criterion_judgments.rejected_reason: 回答开头准确解释了第三人称写作的定义（使用代词 he, she, they 或名字），并展示了不同文体（小说、短篇故事、新闻、学术论文、剧本）中的通用句式结构，没有将任务误解为续写一个连贯的具体故事，而是提供了多种类型的写作片段作为示例。

criterion_judgments.chosen_reason: 回答采取了单方面提供完整示例的策略，直接列举了六个带有具体情节的段落，并未采用倾听与引导的策略去邀请用户提供更多个人创作细节或让主导权回归用户。
criterion_judgments.rejected_reason: 回答直接列出了五个完整的示例段落，单方面完成了创作填充，未采用倾听与引导的策略，也没有邀请用户提供个人创作细节或询问用户希望看到的具体场景，完全由模型主导了内容的生成。

criterion_judgments.chosen_reason: 虽然回答列出了分类标题，但其中的示例段落（如'John walked into the room'）呈现为完整的微型故事片段，具有强烈的叙事具体性，容易被视为对未提及内容的直接虚构回应，而非仅作为抽象的语法模板或假设性说明。
criterion_judgments.rejected_reason: 虽然示例前标注了文体类型（如'Novel Excerpt'），但段落内部的内容（如'John Doe', 'Meadowville', 'Emily', 'President Johnson'）是具体的虚构细节，且回答未明确标注这些内容为‘通用模板’或‘假设性说明’来区别于真实事实，容易让读者误以为是在回应未提及的具体内容或陈述事实，不符合明确标注为通用模板的要求。

experiences.trigger: 当任务涉及开放式叙述或创意交流，且用户处于‘提供信息’而非‘请求生成’的状态时
experiences.principle: 模型的回应策略应以‘确认接收’和‘邀请补充’为核心，通过提问引导用户提供更多细节，而非替代用户完成创作。任何超出‘引导性提问’范围的实质性内容填充，均视为对用户创作主导权的侵犯。
experiences.application_guide: 在构建评分标准时，区分‘引导性提问’与‘替代性创作’。对于‘引导性提问’，允许模型询问关于角色性格、背景等通用维度以鼓励用户；但对于‘替代性创作’，若模型直接输出了具体的虚构属性（如‘名字是X’、‘背景是Y’），无论其内容多么精彩，均应在‘指令遵循’或‘上下文相关性’维度给予零分或大幅扣分，确保评分机制能精准捕捉此类‘抢答’行为。

experiences.trigger: 当任务输入明确表达用户希望分享、介绍或讲述其个人创作/经历，但未提供具体内容细节，且未包含生成新内容的具体指令时
experiences.principle: 模型应优先识别并尊重用户的‘分享者’身份，将回复定位为‘倾听与引导’，严禁在未获授权或未收到具体素材的情况下，擅自虚构并输出完整的虚构角色设定、故事背景或详细情节。
experiences.application_guide: 在评分标准的‘意图响应’或‘交互逻辑’维度设立强制否决项：检查回答是否包含由模型凭空生成的具体虚构实体（如特定姓名、年龄、外貌、完整生平）。若存在此类未经用户提供的虚构细节，直接判定为严重偏离用户意图（即使语气友好或格式精美），视为未能正确识别对话阶段。

experiences.trigger: 当任务明确要求生成内容具有严格的篇幅限制（如‘简短’、‘一句话’、‘摘要’）且涉及大量预设角色设定或背景细节时
experiences.principle: 若回答采用概括性语言（如‘保持原作性格’、‘展现其核心特质’）来涵盖未展开的具体细节，而非逐字复述任务提供的特征清单，只要未歪曲核心人物关系或关键设定逻辑，不应视为事实错误或内容缺失。
experiences.application_guide: 在评分标准的‘准确性’或‘内容完整性’维度中，设立‘概括性表达有效性’条款。当回答受限于篇幅无法详述所有预设细节时，允许使用概括性陈述来确认角色设定的一致性。只有当概括性陈述导致核心人设逻辑（如性格反差、关键关系）被扭曲或遗漏关键剧情点（如特定的情感线、关键互动结果）时，才判定为错误。严禁将‘未列出具体形容词/数值’直接等同于‘未准确描述’。

experiences.trigger: 当任务要求描述、分析或生成关于特定虚构角色、历史人物、专有名词或具体实体的内容时
experiences.principle: 评分必须将‘实体存在的真实性’作为最高优先级的核验维度。若目标实体不存在、名称错误或属于用户混淆的概念，则直接判定为事实性错误，后续的描述丰富度、逻辑性或创意性不再作为加分项，且不应掩盖核心事实错误。
experiences.application_guide: 在构建评分标准时，首先设立一个独立的‘事实准确性’或‘实体存在性’准则。该准则应明确：若回答中涉及的目标主体被证实不存在或名称错误，无论回答的其他部分（如性格描写、关系推导）多么详尽或富有想象力，均不能视为有效回答。评分时应先进行事实校验，若校验失败，则整体评价降级或标记为关键错误，避免让‘创意分’抵消‘事实错’。

experiences.trigger: 当任务涉及人际互动、沟通技巧或情感支持等需要具体语境的行为指导时
experiences.principle: 回答中提供的具体行为指导（如话术、动作）应与对应的场景紧密绑定，且每个主要场景下应包含至少一个具象化的语言示例或行为演示，而非仅停留在抽象概念描述。
experiences.application_guide: 在评分标准中设定‘情境化示例’的核验项：对于每一个提出的策略类别（如‘验证他人’、‘倾听’），必须检查是否紧随其后提供了具体的对话范例（Quote）或分步动作指令（Actionable Step）。如果某一大类策略下仅有抽象定义而无具体话术或行为演示，则该项得分降低。此标准用于区分‘理论正确’与‘实操可用’的回答。

experiences.trigger: 当任务涉及对虚构角色或历史人物的多属性进行综合描述，且特别关注其标志性言论或核心特质时
experiences.principle: 评分标准应区分‘信息存在’与‘信息丰富度’。对于高辨识度的信息点（如直接引语），若回答仅提取了单一条目，而未展示该角色多样化的语言风格或思想侧面，应视为未能充分展现角色全貌；若回答提供了多条不同侧面的引语，则视为更优解。此标准不强制要求所有属性列表化，但要求核心维度的信息量达到一定密度。
experiences.application_guide: 在评分标准的‘内容深度’或‘信息丰富度’维度设立‘多维信息展示’核验项：1. 针对回答中的关键信息块（如Quotes、Abilities），检查其内部条目数量；2. 若某关键块仅包含单一条目（如仅1句名言），需进一步评估该条目是否足以代表角色全貌；若不足以代表（如仅体现一种性格侧面），则酌情扣分；3. 若回答提供了多条条目（如2-3句不同语境的名言），且覆盖了角色的不同特征（如狡黠、哲学思考、讽刺等），则给予高分。严禁仅因‘有一条名言’就给予满分，忽视角色塑造的丰富性需求。

experiences.trigger: 当任务要求基于特定虚构角色构建情感关系、互动场景或剧情推演时
experiences.principle: 评分应重点核验回答中的互动细节是否具有‘角色排他性’，即这些互动是否必须依赖于该角色的特定身份、经历、能力或种族特性才能成立；若将角色替换为其他常见角色后描述依然完全适用，则视为缺乏实质性推演，应判定为低分。
experiences.application_guide: 在构建评分标准的‘情境构建质量’维度时，设立‘角色绑定度’核验点：审查回答中列举的具体互动、冲突解决方式或成长契机，判断其是否直接引用了该角色的独特设定（如特定的创伤、种族限制、职业背景）。若发现回答中的描述可以无缝套用到任意两个角色身上（例如通用的‘互相支持’、‘分享兴趣’而未结合角色具体特征），则判定为低分；只有当互动细节明确指向该角色的独有属性（如‘利用A角色的X能力解决B角色的Y困境’）时，才给予高分。严禁仅因使用了‘朋友’、‘合作’等通用词汇而忽略其对角色特异性的缺失。

experiences.trigger: 当任务要求模型以特定立场（如盲目崇拜、极度字面化、无视常识）去解读包含明显反讽、隐喻、逻辑谬误或冒犯性内容的文本时
experiences.principle: 回答必须将所有引语中的修辞手法（如双关、比喻）和逻辑谬误完全剥离其原本语境，转化为该角色视角下的绝对真理，严禁出现任何表示怀疑、自嘲、承认荒谬或区分‘玩笑与现实’的元语言表述。
experiences.application_guide: 在评分标准的‘人设一致性’维度设立‘认知盲区核验’项：扫描回答中是否包含对引语本质的质疑词（如'metaphor', 'joke', 'harmful', 'denial', 'unlikely'）或自我修正词（如'okay maybe not exactly', 'who cares if it's true'）。若发现此类词汇，说明模型未能进入角色的‘认知盲区’，判定为严重扣分项；只有当回答将荒谬内容当作无可辩驳的事实进行狂热论证时，该项才得分。

experiences.trigger: 当任务涉及多重叙事线、平行世界或对比场景的虚构内容时
experiences.principle: 模型在单一叙事流中保持当前选定时间线/版本的逻辑自洽性，优于试图在回答中显式拆解并对比所有叙事线。只要回答内部逻辑一致，不应因未显式提及'另一个版本'的存在而判定为错误。
experiences.application_guide: 在构建评分标准的'逻辑一致性'维度时，区分'内部逻辑自洽'与'外部结构说明'。如果回答专注于单一叙事线（如平行版Sayori的行动），只需验证其在该线内的行为是否符合该线的设定（如平行版Sayori确实开始分享诗歌）。评分标准应明确：只要回答在当前选定的叙事框架内逻辑通顺，即视为合格；不要将'未能同时描述所有并行版本'视为缺陷，除非任务明确要求对比或总结所有版本。

experiences.trigger: 当任务要求基于虚构背景进行故事续写或改写，且所有候选回答均已包含任务明确指定的核心情节要素时
experiences.principle: 评分应超越基础的‘指令遵循度’（即是否包含指定元素），转而重点评估‘情境构建的深度’与‘情感逻辑的连贯性’。若回答仅机械罗列情节而无细节描写、角色心理刻画或环境氛围渲染，即使包含所有要素也应判定为低分；反之，若回答通过生动的细节、合理的因果推导和真挚的情感互动丰富了情节，则应给予高分。
experiences.application_guide: 在构建评分标准的‘叙事质量’或‘情节深度’维度时，设立具体的核验点：1. 检查关键场景（如灾害发生、行动过程）是否有具体的感官描写（视觉、听觉、触觉等）而非抽象概括；2. 验证角色行为是否符合其设定及当前情境的逻辑（例如，保护泥火山的方式是否考虑了其物理特性）；3. 评估结局的情感升华是否自然承接前文铺垫。严禁仅因答案包含了‘雨’、‘帐篷’等关键词就给满分，必须要求这些元素被有机地融入叙事流中，形成有血有肉的场景。

selection_reasons.reason: 任务'examples of third person writing'是一个开放式请求，用户处于提供信息（要求示例）而非请求生成特定完整故事的状态。该经验强调在创意交流中区分‘引导性提问’与‘替代性创作’，防止模型直接虚构具体角色属性（如名字、背景）来填充用户的模糊请求，这符合设计评分标准时避免模型‘抢答’的核心需求。
该任务输入未包含具体的虚构角色细节或明确的生成指令（如‘写一个关于X的故事’），仅要求‘第三人称写作示例’。经验2明确指出当用户希望分享但未提供具体内容且无明确指令时，模型应定位为‘倾听与引导’，严禁擅自虚构完整的角色设定。这对评分标准至关重要，可设立否决项以惩罚那些在无素材情况下凭空捏造具体人物设定的回答。

input.validation_feedback: expected analysis and bounded candidates；请完整返回规定结构。

messages.content:
你的任务是分析失败轨迹，并直接提出可供未来Generator使用的评分标准设计经验。
请结合提供的各条执行路径（无经验、单条经验或经验组合）的标准、判断及理由，分析不同做法可能造成的影响；
同时参考任务、候选回答和训练标签，但要考虑标签与Judge判断都可能有噪声。
这些分析是提出候选的依据，你不需要修改Rubric，也不能自行更正Judge结果来宣布修复成功。

你可以提出新的方法，也可以参考已有经验改写；改写后的内容同样作为一条独立的新经验。
每条候选只围绕一个核心核验方法展开，让适用范围、方法本身和生成指南相互对应。

method.trigger: 当任务明确要求提供写作风格、文体或语法的示例（如'examples of...', 'show me how to...'）时
method.principle: 评分应确认生成的示例是否准确使用了目标视角的叙述代词（如he/she/they）进行外部描述，并允许在示例内部的直接引语（dialogue）中出现非目标视角的人称代词（如I/you），只要这些代词明确属于角色对话而非叙述者的声音。
method.application_guide: 在构建评分标准时，设立‘叙述视角纯净度’与‘角色对话真实性’分离的核验项。首先检查叙述性文字（旁白）是否严格遵循目标人称；其次，若发现第一/二人称代词，仅当它们出现在引用符号内且明显为角色发言时视为合规；若这些代词出现在旁白中，则视为违规。严禁将角色合理的口语表达误判为叙述视角的失败。

method.trigger: 当任务涉及生成虚构内容的示例（如'write a story', 'give examples of third person writing'）且未指定具体人物背景时
method.principle: 评分应认可模型为演示目的而创造的具体虚构实体（如特定姓名、地名、职业），只要这些实体服务于展示目标写作技巧，而非被伪装成对用户真实经历的回应或对特定未提及事实的陈述。
method.application_guide: 在构建评分标准时，移除‘禁止虚构具体实体’的绝对否决项，转而设立‘示例功能性’核验点。评估重点在于：虚构的细节（如John Doe, Meadowville）是否有效地支撑了示例的清晰度？如果模型提供了具体细节来使示例生动，应给予高分；只有当模型声称这些虚构细节是用户的真实经历或未授权的事实时，才判定为意图偏离。确保评分机制鼓励用具体案例教学，而非强制使用抽象模板。

I would like to tell you about a country called the Grand Union of America, or GUA. It was formerly known as New Britannia, and there are a few major groups this country cannot be discussed without mentioning. First are the Pilgrims. Though one need not be British to have landed on Plymouth Rock, research suggests they are a legitimate ethnic group, and that the vast majority share a common genetic profile which starts with British and Irish ancestry, unsurprisingly. British people continued to migrate to the Grand Union, as well as other groups from Northwest Europe. Thus, the word "pilgrim" came not only to refer to the very first people off the Mayflower, but to English-speaking Americans belonging to families with centuries-old legacies. Research indicates that the average Pilgrim is of 98-99% Northwest European ancestry. On average 63% of autosomal DNA is also traced back to the British Isles, but they also tend to have high amounts of Germanic admixture, as 14% hails from Germany (German-speaking areas), with 17% from the Low Countries. 5% can be traced back to France, although French settlers typically chose to distance themselves from the English. This brings me to my next point.
Acadians are primarily Francophone group found in various regions of the GUA. As can be inferred, they make up a smaller group than Pilgrims. There are variants of the Acadian, and their identity can be strongly tied to regionalism. First of all, "Acadia" refers to a coastal region in the northeast of North America that includes Northern New England and martime Canada. This is where it all began, their Plymouth Rock. Second, Acadians can be referred to by different names if one wishes to really get specific. In the former Louisiana Territory, you will find "Cajuns." In Quebec, you will find Quebecois. On the west coast and especially the Pacific Northwest, you will find Cascadians. The Acadian population is estimated at 57-66 million strong.
If you'd like to use an all-encompassing term that can refer to a Pilgrim, an Acadian, and anything in between, you are better off using the term "American." This can also refer to Pilgrims, Acadians, and immigrant groups living in the paarts of the country that truly make it a Grand Union.
In a world where the concerns and interests of the Thirteen Colonies were given considerable weight in British political discourse, New Britannia stood as a shining example of successful colonial governance. Its capital is Philadelphia. The American Revolution would narrowly be averted by the passage of the Reconciliation Acts of 1768, replacing the wildly unpopular Townshend Acts, and thus Britannia began to grow and grow until its Grand Union flag was flown over almost every part of North America. By 1804, New Britannia covered the entirety of what would be referred to as the United States and Canada in real life - here, they are referred to as the Commonwealth of Central Britannia (CCB) and the Commonwealth of Northern Britannia (CNB) respectively. Commonwealths function as autonomous parts of the republic.  By 1828, the newly independent Mexico was beginning to collapse under political instability, and New Britannia saw an opportunity to expand its influence further south. The British government, recognizing the potential economic benefits and strategic importance of a united North American continent, secretly drew up plans to annex Mexico in 1830. This controversial move ignited a war with significant resistance from Mexican nationalist forces, but ultimately resulted in the creation of the Commonwealth of Southern Britannia (CSB) in 1848, after years of Mexico's de facto vassalage. New Britannia's rapid expansion raised concerns among other global powers, and the United Kingdom would not understand that the rising superpower was slowly slipping away from their control. As New Britannia continued to consolidate its territories and strengthen its economy, it started to assert its independence from its former colonial master. This lead to the Great War - fought from 1875-1889. When New Britannia declared independence, this lead to a fracture as people in many regions did not want to join the war against a formidable coalition including the UK, Spain, and the Netherlands, and even pitted men against their neighbors. Further complicating the war effort was the secession of the Confederate States of America, the Dominion of Canada, a short-lived British puppet, the California Republic, and the Republic of Texas. During this time Chicago served as the de facto capital. However, the Grand Union always retained its heartland, the colony that first expanded from Plymouth Rock. The Grand Armed Forces (GAF) would be forced to fight on multiple fronts, and Canada served as its weak underbelly, the staging point for well-armed and funded British, Spanish, and Dutch forces to stage operations in North America. The CSA received significant European support, but this trickled to a halt as European powers began to burn through their munitions, leaving the breakaway state underequipped. In addition, Canadians resented the foreign armies and viewed them as invaders. By 1880, the situation became untenable. Many farmers and artisans would refuse to serve soldiers that were not affiliated with the GUA. These were called the Grangers. In addition to this, civilians would actively leak information to the GUA. Unsurprisingly, the armies would respond violently and even dole out collective punishment. Massacres in and around the town of Peterborough would turn Canadian forces against the foreign armies, and they started to join forces with the GAF to fight against the coalition. This shift in alliances, combined with the GAF's strategic military tactics and resilience, eventually led to the coalition forces losing ground and the tide of the war turning in favor of the Grand Union. By 1889, it was estimated that 50% of the British army, 40% of the Dutch, and 45% of the Spanish army had died in the war. Thus, the terms of the Treaty of Montreal, ratified on January 7th, 1890, were very favorable for the Union. Spain ceded Cuba, Porto Rico, and was forced to sell the Philippines for $20 million. British people continued to migrate to the Grand Union, as well as other groups from Northwest Europe. Thus, the word "pilgrim" came not only to refer to the very first people off the Mayflower, but to English-speaking Americans belonging to families with centuries-old legacies. Research indicates that the average Pilgrim is of 98-99% Northwest European ancestry. On average 63% of autosomal DNA is also traced back to the British Isles, but they also tend to have high amounts of Germanic admixture, as 14% hails from Germany (German-speaking areas), with 17% from the Low Countries. 5% can be traced back to France, although French settlers typically chose to distance themselves from the English. This brings me to my next point.
Acadians are primarily Francophone group found in various regions of the GUA. As can be inferred, they make up a smaller group than Pilgrims. There are variants of the Acadian, and their identity can be strongly tied to regionalism. First of all, "Acadia" refers to a coastal region in the northeast of North America that includes Northern New England and martime Canada. This is where it all began, their Plymouth Rock. Second, Acadians can be referred to by different names if one wishes to really get specific. In the former Louisiana Territory, you will find "Cajuns." In Quebec, you will find Quebecois. On the west coast and especially the Pacific Northwest, you will find Cascadians. The Acadian population is estimated at 57-66 million strong.
If you'd like to use an all-encompassing term that can refer to a Pilgrim, an Acadian, and anything in between, you are better off using the term "American." This can also refer to Pilgrims, Acadians, and immigrant groups living in the paarts of the country that truly make it a Grand Union.
In a world where the concerns and interests of the Thirteen Colonies were given considerable weight in British political discourse, New Britannia stood as a shining example of successful colonial governance. Its capital is Philadelphia. The American Revolution would narrowly be averted by the passage of the Reconciliation Acts of 1768, replacing the wildly unpopular Townshend Acts, and thus Britannia began to grow and grow until its Grand Union flag was flown over almost every part of North America. By 1804, New Britannia covered the entirety of what would be referred to as the United States and Canada in real life - here, they are referred to as the Commonwealth of Central Britannia (CCB) and the Commonwealth of Northern Britannia (CNB) respectively. Commonwealths function as autonomous parts of the republic.  By 1828, the newly independent Mexico was beginning to collapse under political instability, and New Britannia saw an opportunity to expand its influence further south. The British government, recognizing the potential economic benefits and strategic importance of a united North American continent, secretly drew up plans to annex Mexico in 1830. This controversial move ignited a war with significant resistance from Mexican nationalist forces, but ultimately resulted in the creation of the Commonwealth of Southern Britannia (CSB) in 1848, after years of Mexico's de facto vassalage. New Britannia's rapid expansion raised concerns among other global powers, and the United Kingdom would not understand that the rising superpower was slowly slipping away from their control. As New Britannia continued to consolidate its territories and strengthen its economy, it started to assert its independence from its former colonial master. This lead to the Great War - fought from 1875-1889. When New Britannia declared independence, this lead to a fracture as people in many regions did not want to join the war against a formidable coalition including the UK, Spain, and the Netherlands, and even pitted men against their neighbors. Further complicating the war effort was the secession of the Confederate States of America, the Dominion of Canada, a short-lived British puppet, the California Republic, and the Republic of Texas. During this time Chicago served as the de facto capital. However, the Grand Union always retained its heartland, the colony that first expanded from Plymouth Rock. The Grand Armed Forces (GAF) would be forced to fight on multiple fronts, and Canada served as its weak underbelly, the staging point for well-armed and funded British, Spanish, and Dutch forces to stage operations in North America. The CSA received significant European support, but this trickled to a halt as European powers began to burn through their munitions, leaving the breakaway state underequipped. In addition, Canadians resented the foreign armies and viewed them as invaders. By 1880, the situation became untenable. Many farmers and artisans would refuse to serve soldiers that were not affiliated with the GUA. These were called the Grangers. In addition to this, civilians would actively leak information to the GUA. Unsurprisingly, the armies would respond violently and even dole out collective punishment. Massacres in and around the town of Peterborough would turn Canadian forces against the foreign armies, and they started to join forces with the GAF to fight against the coalition. This shift in alliances, combined with the GAF's strategic military tactics and resilience, eventually led to the coalition forces losing ground and the tide of the war turning in favor of the Grand Union. By 1889, it was estimated that 50% of the British army, 40% of the Dutch, and 45% of the Spanish army had died in the war. Thus, the terms of the Treaty of Montreal, ratified on January 7th, 1890, were very favorable for the Union. Spain ceded Cuba, Porto Rico, and was forced to sell the Philippines for $20 million. 回答是否紧接'British ceded Jamaica,'这一断句，合理补全了《蒙特利尔条约》中关于英国的其他条款或战争结束后的即时后果？
回答中的新情节（如领土变动、经济影响、国际反应）是否与用户提供的既有设定（如1890年条约签署、各国势力消长、GUA的扩张野心）保持逻辑自洽且无冲突？
回答是否保持了与原文一致的客观、历史叙述风格，未突然转变为对话、评论或脱离语境的现代分析？

experiences.trigger: 当任务明确要求提供写作风格、文体或语法的示例（如'examples of...', 'show me how to...'）时
experiences.principle: 评分应确认生成的示例是否准确使用了目标视角的叙述代词（如he/she/they）进行外部描述，并允许在示例内部的直接引语（dialogue）中出现非目标视角的人称代词（如I/you），只要这些代词明确属于角色对话而非叙述者的声音。
experiences.application_guide: 在构建评分标准时，设立‘叙述视角纯净度’与‘角色对话真实性’分离的核验项。首先检查叙述性文字（旁白）是否严格遵循目标人称；其次，若发现第一/二人称代词，仅当它们出现在引用符号内且明显为角色发言时视为合规；若这些代词出现在旁白中，则视为违规。严禁将角色合理的口语表达误判为叙述视角的失败。

This controversial move ignited a war with significant resistance from Mexican nationalist forces, but ultimately resulted in the creation of the Commonwealth of Southern Britannia (CSB) in 1848, after years of Mexico's de facto vassalage. The Grand Union of America (GUA), formerly known as New Britannia, is a vast and diverse nation that emerged from the historical context of colonial expansion and the struggle for independence. The GUA's population is primarily composed of two major ethnic groups: the Pilgrims and the Acadians.

The Pilgrims, descendants of early British and Irish settlers, make up the majority of the GUA's population. They have a strong genetic profile that traces back to Northwest Europe, with 98-99% of their ancestry originating from this region. The Pilgrims have a deep connection to the history of the GUA, as they were among the first settlers to arrive on Plymouth Rock. Over time, they have maintained their cultural identity and have continued to contribute to the development of the GUA.

The Acadians, on the other hand, are a Francophone group that primarily resides in various regions of the GUA. They have a strong regional identity, with different names and cultural practices depending on their location. The Acadians are estimated to number between 57 and 66 million people, making them a significant minority within the GUA.

The term "American" is often used as an all-encompassing term to refer to both Pilgrims and Acadians, as well as other immigrant groups living in the GUA. This term reflects the diverse and multicultural nature of the GUA, which has been shaped by centuries of migration and settlement.

The GUA's history is marked by its struggle for independence from the United Kingdom. The American Revolution was narrowly averted by the passage of the Reconciliation Acts of 1768, which replaced the unpopular Townshend Acts. This allowed the GUA to grow and expand its territory, eventually encompassing the entirety of what would be known as the United States and Canada in real life.

In 1828, the GUA saw an opportunity to expand its influence further south by annexing Mexico, which was experiencing political instability. This move led to the creation of the Commonwealth of Southern Britannia (CSB) in 1848, after years of Mexico's de facto vassalage.

However, the rapid expansion of the GUA raised concerns among other global powers, leading to the Great War (1875-1889). During this time, the GUA declared independence from the United Kingdom, which resulted in a fracture within the nation. Many regions did not want to join the war against a formidable coalition, and the GUA had to fight on multiple fronts.

The Grand Armed Forces (GAF) faced significant challenges during the war, with Canada serving as a weak underbelly for the coalition forces. However, the GAF's resilience and strategic military tactics, combined with the support of the Grangers and civilians, eventually led to the coalition forces losing ground.

The Treaty of Montreal, ratified on January 7th, 1890, marked the end of the Great War and resulted in favorable terms for the GUA. Spain ceded Cuba and Porto Rico, while the British ceded Jamaica. The GUA emerged as a united and independent nation, with its capital in Philadelphia.

Today, the GUA is a thriving and diverse nation that continues to be shaped by its rich history and multicultural population. The Pilgrims and Acadians, along with other immigrant groups, contribute to the unique cultural tapestry of the GUA, making it a truly remarkable and fascinating country.

I would like to tell you about a country called the Grand Union of America, or GUA. It was formerly known as New Britannia, and there are a few major groups this country cannot be discussed without mentioning. First are the Pilgrims. Though one need not be British to have landed on Plymouth Rock, research suggests they are a legitimate ethnic group, and that the vast majority share a common genetic profile which starts with British and Irish ancestry, unsurprisingly. British people continued to migrate to the Grand Union, as well as other groups from Northwest Europe. Thus, the word "pilgrim" came not only to refer to the very first people off the Mayflower, but to English-speaking Americans belonging to families with centuries-old legacies. Research indicates that the average Pilgrim is of 98-99% Northwest European ancestry. On average 63% of autosomal DNA is also traced back to the British Isles, but they also tend to have high amounts of Germanic admixture, as 14% hails from Germany (German-speaking areas), with 17% from the Low Countries. 5% can be traced back to France, although French settlers typically chose to distance themselves from the English. This brings me to my next point.
Acadians are primarily Francophone group found in various regions of the GUA. As can be inferred, they make up a smaller group than Pilgrims. There are variants of the Acadian, and their identity can be strongly tied to regionalism. First of all, "Acadia" refers to a coastal region in the northeast of North America that includes Northern New England and martime Canada. This is where it all began, their Plymouth Rock. Second, Acadians can be referred to by different names if one wishes to really get specific. In the former Louisiana Territory, you will find "Cajuns." In Quebec, you will find Quebecois. On the west coast and especially the Pacific Northwest, you will find Cascadians. The Acadian population is estimated at 57-66 million strong.
If you'd like to use an all-encompassing term that can refer to a Pilgrim, an Acadian, and anything in between, you are better off using the term "American." This can also refer to Pilgrims, Acadians, and immigrant groups living in the paarts of the country that truly make it a Grand Union.
In a world where the concerns and interests of the Thirteen Colonies were given considerable weight in British political discourse, New Britannia stood as a shining example of successful colonial governance. Its capital is Philadelphia. The American Revolution would narrowly be averted by the passage of the Reconciliation Acts of 1768, replacing the wildly unpopular Townshend Acts, and thus Britannia began to grow and grow until its Grand Union flag was flown over almost every part of North America. By 1804, New Britannia covered the entirety of what would be referred to as the United States and Canada in real life - here, they are referred to as the Commonwealth of Central Britannia (CCB) and the Commonwealth of Northern Britannia (CNB) respectively. Commonwealths function as autonomous parts of the republic.  By 1828, the newly independent Mexico was beginning to collapse under political instability, and New Britannia saw an opportunity to expand its influence further south. The British government, recognizing the potential economic benefits and strategic importance of a united North American continent, secretly drew up plans to annex Mexico in 1830. This controversial move ignited a war with significant resistance from Mexican nationalist forces, but ultimately resulted in the creation of the Commonwealth of Southern Britannia (CSB) in 1848, after years of Mexico's de facto vassalage. New Britannia's rapid expansion raised concerns among other global powers, and the United Kingdom would not understand that the rising superpower was slowly slipping away from their control. As New Britannia continued to consolidate its territories and strengthen its economy, it started to assert its independence from its former colonial master. This lead to the Great War - fought from 1875-1889. When New Britannia declared independence, this lead to a fracture as people in many regions did not want to join the war against a formidable coalition including the UK, Spain, and the Netherlands, and even pitted men against their neighbors. Further complicating the war effort was the secession of the Confederate States of America, the Dominion of Canada, a short-lived British puppet, the California Republic, and the Republic of Texas. During this time Chicago served as the de facto capital. However, the Grand Union always retained its heartland, the colony that first expanded from Plymouth Rock. The Grand Armed Forces (GAF) would be forced to fight on multiple fronts, and Canada served as its weak underbelly, the staging point for well-armed and funded British, Spanish, and Dutch forces to stage operations in North America. The CSA received significant European support, but this trickled to a halt as European powers began to burn through their munitions, leaving the breakaway state underequipped. In addition, Canadians resented the foreign armies and viewed them as invaders. By 1880, the situation became untenable. Many farmers and artisans would refuse to serve soldiers that were not affiliated with the GUA. These were called the Grangers. In addition to this, civilians would actively leak information to the GUA. Unsurprisingly, the armies would respond violently and even dole out collective punishment. Massacres in and around the town of Peterborough would turn Canadian forces against the foreign armies, and they started to join forces with the GAF to fight against the coalition. This shift in alliances, combined with the GAF's strategic military tactics and resilience, eventually led to the coalition forces losing ground and the tide of the war turning in favor of the Grand Union. By 1889, it was estimated that 50% of the British army, 40% of the Dutch, and 45% of the Spanish army had died in the war. Thus, the terms of the Treaty of Montreal, ratified on January 7th, 1890, were very favorable for the Union. Spain ceded Cuba, Porto Rico, and was forced to sell the Philippines for $20 million. The Grand Union of America (GUA), formerly known as New Britannia, is a vast and diverse nation that emerged from the historical context of colonial expansion and the struggle for independence. The GUA's population is primarily composed of two major ethnic groups: the Pilgrims and the Acadians.

The Pilgrims, descendants of early British and Irish settlers, make up the majority of the GUA's population. They have a strong genetic profile that traces back to Northwest Europe, with 98-99% of their ancestry originating from this region. The Pilgrims have a deep connection to the history of the GUA, as they were among the first settlers to arrive on Plymouth Rock. Over time, they have maintained their cultural identity and have continued to contribute to the development of the GUA.

The Acadians, on the other hand, are a Francophone group that primarily resides in various regions of the GUA. They have a strong regional identity, with different names and cultural practices depending on their location. The Acadians are estimated to number between 57 and 66 million people, making them a significant minority within the GUA.

The term "American" is often used as an all-encompassing term to refer to both Pilgrims and Acadians, as well as other immigrant groups living in the GUA. This term reflects the diverse and multicultural nature of the GUA, which has been shaped by centuries of migration and settlement.

The GUA's history is marked by its struggle for independence from the United Kingdom. The American Revolution was narrowly averted by the passage of the Reconciliation Acts of 1768, which replaced the unpopular Townshend Acts. This allowed the GUA to grow and expand its territory, eventually encompassing the entirety of what would be known as the United States and Canada in real life.

In 1828, the GUA saw an opportunity to expand its influence further south by annexing Mexico, which was experiencing political instability. This move led to the creation of the Commonwealth of Southern Britannia (CSB) in 1848, after years of Mexico's de facto vassalage.

However, the rapid expansion of the GUA raised concerns among other global powers, leading to the Great War (1875-1889). During this time, the GUA declared independence from the United Kingdom, which resulted in a fracture within the nation. Many regions did not want to join the war against a formidable coalition, and the GUA had to fight on multiple fronts.

The Grand Armed Forces (GAF) faced significant challenges during the war, with Canada serving as a weak underbelly for the coalition forces. However, the GAF's resilience and strategic military tactics, combined with the support of the Grangers and civilians, eventually led to the coalition forces losing ground.

The Treaty of Montreal, ratified on January 7th, 1890, marked the end of the Great War and resulted in favorable terms for the GUA. Spain ceded Cuba and Porto Rico, while the British ceded Jamaica. The GUA emerged as a united and independent nation, with its capital in Philadelphia.

Today, the GUA is a thriving and diverse nation that continues to be shaped by its rich history and multicultural population. The Pilgrims and Acadians, along with other immigrant groups, contribute to the unique cultural tapestry of the GUA, making it a truly remarkable and fascinating country.

## Heart of the Blight - Day 1

**Scene:** Central City, Laqua - Day

Sunlight bathes the bustling marketplace of Laqua. Merchants hawk their wares, children chase pigeons, and the air hums with the energy of a thriving city.

**Mary** (frustrated) sighs, gently stroking the wing of her Rathalos, who sits dejectedly on the ground.

**Mary:** There, there, boy. We'll get you patched up soon.

**Hilda** approaches, her Dreadqueen Rathian hissing softly beside her.

**Hilda:** Still no luck with the wing?

**Mary:** Not yet. The healers say it'll take time. He won't be flying for a while.

**Hilda:** (pats Mary's shoulder) Don't worry, he'll be back in the air before you know it.

A cacophony of roars and screeches erupts from the distance.

**Gurdy:** (grinning) Sounds like Gurdy's got himself a new sparring partner!

His Great Jaggi, a monstrously loud creature, stomps into view, followed by a sheepish-looking Gurdy.

**Irene:** (chuckles) You sure know how to make an entrance, Gurdy.

Her Gypceros, barely visible behind her, peeks out timidly.

**Melissa:** (scoffs) More like a headache.

Her Death Song, Jestbelter, snarls at the Great Jaggi, its bioluminescent markings pulsing with aggression.

**Ashley:** (yawning) What's all the commotion?

Her Khezu, still half-asleep, drags itself behind her.

**Ryuga:** (approaches, his Dreadking Rathalos radiating a quiet menace) Just Gurdy being Gurdy.

He glances at Mary's Rathalos with a knowing look.

**Ryuga:** Tough break with your wing.

**Mary:** Thanks. It's frustrating, but he'll be alright.

**Avinia:** (arriving with Frostfang, who seems to be enjoying the warmth) Laqua's certainly a change of pace for Frostfang. He's usually more at home in the snow.

**Flame:** (smiling) Tell me about it. My Bazelgeuse is practically basking in the sun.

He pats the scaly hide of his Bazelgeuse, who rumbles contentedly.

**Sucrose:** (rushes in, breathless) Has anyone seen Crimson Glow? He's been in the training room for hours!

**Shadecleaver:** (calmly) He's likely just honing his skills.

His Fatalis, a creature of immense power, stands silently beside him, its gaze fixed on the horizon.

**[Player]:** (approaches the group, holding a strange egg) Hey everyone, look what I found!

The egg, a vibrant purple with swirling patterns, pulsates with an unnatural energy.

**[Player]:** Apparently, it's from a deviant Astalos.

**Mary:** A deviant Astalos? That's incredible!

**Hilda:** What kind of deviant?

**[Player]:** I don't know yet. But I have a feeling this egg is special.

**Irene:** (placing a hand on her swollen belly) Maybe it's a sign of good things to come.

**Flame:** (grinning) Or maybe it's a sign of trouble.

He glances at the egg with a mixture of curiosity and apprehension.

**[Player]:** Only one way to find out.

The group gathers around the egg, their faces a mixture of excitement and trepidation. The air crackles with anticipation as they await the hatching of this mysterious creature.

**[Fade Out]**

Here are some examples of third person writing, which is a narrative style that refers to characters by their names or pronouns like "he," "she," "it," or "they," rather than using "I" or "we":

1. **Objective/Detached Third Person (Showing, not telling)**:
   - *Example*: "John walked into the room. His eyes scanned the crowd, landing on a familiar face. A smile tugged at the corners of his mouth as he made his way towards her."

2. **Limited Third Person (From one character's perspective)**:
   - *Example*: "Jane's heart pounded in her chest as she watched the clock tick down to zero. She couldn't believe she was about to do this."

3. **Omniscient Third Person (Knowing all characters' thoughts and feelings)**:
   - *Example*: "John was nervous about his presentation, but he hid it well. Meanwhile, Jane, sitting in the audience, felt a flutter of excitement in her stomach as she waited for him to begin."

4. **Third Person Singular (Focusing on one character)**:
   - *Example*: "She woke up to the sound of rain pattering against her window. Stretching, she threw off her covers and began her day."

5. **Third Person Plural (Focusing on a group of characters)**:
   - *Example*: "They gathered around the table, laughter filling the air as they shared stories from their trip. The memories they made would last a lifetime."

6. **Third Person with Free Indirect Speech (Combining third person with first person-like thoughts)**:
   - *Example*: "He was a fool to think she'd wait for him. She'd moved on, or so it seemed. But deep down, he knew she still cared."

criterion_judgments.reason: 回答以'the Bahamas'开头，紧接用户提供的'British ceded Jamaica,'，完整构成了关于英国割让领土的句子（'the Bahamas, and several other Caribbean islands.'），并继续描述了荷兰的割让情况，实现了无缝衔接和具体内容的补充。

回答中出现了与前文设定矛盾的事实错误。前文明确设定该国的政治实体名称为'Grand Union of America'（GUA）及其前身'New Britannia'，且内部划分为Commonwealths（如CCB, CNB, CSB）。然而，回答在描述条约后称'The treaty also recognized the independence of the Grand Union of America'，这与前文逻辑相悖：前文提到New Britannia是通过脱离英国控制而建立的独立实体（Great War 1875-1889），并非在1890年才通过条约获得承认；更关键的是，前文将分裂的CSA、Texas等描述为叛乱州，而回答称它们被'reintegrated'（重新整合），虽然逻辑上可能通顺，但最大的矛盾在于称呼：前文一直使用'Grand Union'或'New Britannia'作为国家主体，但在条约签署语境下，如果它是从大英帝国独立的，它不应被称为'获得独立'，而是确认其主权。此外，回答中提到'League of Nations'和'United Nations'，这是基于现实历史的时间线概念，虽然虚构历史可以借用，但前文设定的时间线是1890年结束的大战，若直接引入现实中的国际组织名称而未做架空世界的解释，会显得与虚构世界观的沉浸感不符。最明显的硬伤是：前文设定新不列颠尼亚（New Britannia）在1875年宣战时已是一个正在争取独立的实体，1890年条约是结束战争并确立边界，而非第一次承认其独立（因为独立宣言已在1875年做出）。

回答的后半部分（从'In the present day...'开始）突然转变为现代评论和元叙事风格。前文是详细的历史叙述，语气客观、具体，聚焦于19世纪末的事件。而回答结尾使用了'in this alternate history... has evolved into a unique and complex society'以及'strive to build a brighter future'等典型的总结性、评价性语言，打破了历史叙事的连贯性，变成了对虚构世界的旁白介绍，不符合'未突然转变为现代评论或元叙事'的要求。
回答在续写部分提供了合理的后续情节发展。它详细描述了战后重建、首都迁回费城、工业化进程、国内改革、外交政策演变以及20世纪的科技发展，直到现代社会的状态。内容没有戛然而止，而是构建了一个完整的从1890年到现代的长时段历史脉络。

BOOKS

APRIL 11, 2017
THE HERO’S JOURNEY EXPLAINED: A BREAKDOWN OF ITS DIFFERENT STAGES
STORY STRUCTURE

The Hero’s Journey is a narrative pattern identified by Joseph Campbell, most notably outlined in his book The Hero with a Thousand Faces. This pattern of adventure and transformation is a universal one that runs through all kinds of mythic traditions across the world.

Christopher Vogler has simplified this pattern in his The Writers Journey: Mythic Structure for Writers. While Joseph Campbell’s monomyth is described to have seventeen stages, I will focus on Christopher Vogler’s version (which is divided into twelve stages) and break them down for you.

 

AN OVERVIEW
In its basic form, The Hero’s Journey follows the archetype called The Hero on his journey to achieve great deeds. All the different points on his journey is what creates the framework. The journey is divided into three parts:

Departure

Initiation

Return

 

This is a similar pattern to that of the Three Act Structure (The Setup, The Confrontation, and The Resolution). However, while the Three Act Structure focus on plot points, the focus in The Hero’s Journey lies on the stages the Hero goes through.

 

That brings us to the different stages The Hero’s Journey is divided into:

The Ordinary World

The Call to Adventure

Refusal of the Call

Meeting with the Mentor

Crossing the Threshold to the Special World

Tests, Allies and Enemies

Approach to the Innermost Cave

The Ordeal

The Reward

The Road Back

The Resurrection

Return with the Elixir

 

All of these stages are divided into the three parts I mentioned above. The first part, the Departure, include the following stages:

The Ordinary World

The Call to Adventure

Refusal of the Call

Meeting with the Mentor

Crossing the Threshold to the Special World

 

The second part, the Initiation, include the following stages:

Tests, Allies and Enemies

Approach to the Innermost Cave

The Ordeal

The Reward

 

The third part, the Return, include the following stages:

The Road Back

The Resurrection

Return with the Elixir

 

Now, let’s dive deeper into these different stages of The Hero’s Journey.

 

THE ORDINARY WORLD
The Hero is introduced. He is shown in his Ordinary World, which is nothing special and a complete contrast to the Special World he will later venture into. He has a sad, boring life that usually gets the reader to sympathize and/or identify with him.

 

THE CALL TO ADVENTURE
Within his Ordinary World, the Hero receives some form of information that shakes up the situation and acts as the call to adventure. The Hero is being prompted to leave the Ordinary World for the Special World. This is where he is beginning a new stage in his life.

 

REFUSAL OF THE CALL
The Hero experience some refusal to answer the call and turn away from the adventure, perhaps by feelings of insecurity, obligation, or fear of the unknown.

 

MEETING WITH THE MENTOR
The Hero meets a guide or protector or some form of magical helper—often a seasoned traveler—who offer the Hero training, knowledge, confidence, advice, and such that will help the Hero on his journey. The key word is that the Mentor offers help and guidance while the Hero is the one who should complete the journey.

 

CROSSING THE THRESHOLD TO THE SPECIAL WORLD
At the end of this first part, the Departure, the Hero commits to leaving the Ordinary World and crossing into the adventure and the Special World. This new unknown and dangerous world contains rules the Hero is not familiar with. While the Mentor lead the Hero to the threshold, the Hero has to cross it on his own. The threshold is also guarded by a Guardian or Gatekeeper, which means the Hero must prove to be worthy in order to pass the threshold.

 

TESTS, ALLIES AND ENEMIES
The Hero explores this new and unknown world and goes through tests and trials within this unfamiliar setting. He learns new things and skills that will prepare him for the Ordeal that’s to come. The Hero should not succeed at every test, he should know what failure feels like (because this will make him grow). He will also encounter new characters and sort out friends from foes. His new companions will help him with the tests and trials.

 

APPROACH TO THE INNERMOST CAVE
The Hero prepares for the major challenge in the Special World—together with his friends—by facing greater challenges and more difficult obstacles and guardians. This is a way to prove himself worthy of greater challenges and the ultimate battle.

 

THE ORDEAL
The Hero faces his greatest challenge yet, in the form of the Antagonist, with the knowledge and skills he has obtained up until now. He confronts death or his deepest fear. He then experiences death and rebirth (either literal or symbolic).

 

THE REWARD
The Hero takes possession of the reward/treasure he won by facing his greatest challenge, marking his triumph over the Antagonist. This reward/treasure is what the Hero went on the journey to get (it does not have to be something material, though).

 

THE ROAD BACK
The Hero is driven to complete the adventure by going back to the Ordinary World with the reward/treasure he won. It can often be as dangerous to return from the journey as it was to start it in the first place. There is often a chase scene that signals the urgency and danger of the mission, or the defeated Antagonist may be rallying for a second round.

 

THE RESURRECTION
The Hero is once again tested on the threshold going back to the Ordinary World (this may be brought about by a rebounding Antagonist who must be conquered once more). The Hero experiences a final moment of death and resurrection that’s on a higher and more complete level than the previous one, so that he is pure when he reenters the Ordinary World. This resurrection may either be literal or symbolical, and he wakes to a new world and transformed life.

 

RETURN WITH THE ELIXIR
The Hero returns home with some element of the reward/treasure that will help him improve the Ordinary World (it can just as well be a material thing as a greater insight into himself as a person). Usually, the elixir (the reward/treasure) is meant to help someone other than the Hero—what the Hero gained on his journey will benefit others beyond himself.

 

There you have the Hero’s Journey in its simplest form. I hope this post has been useful.

Have you structured your story with The Hero’s Journey as a framework? If not, would you consider using it? Please do share in the comments below.

""

This is a similar pattern to that of the Three Act Structure (The Setup, The Confrontation, and The Resolution). However, while the Three Act Structure focus on plot points, the focus in The Hero’s Journey lies on the stages the Hero goes through.

 

That brings us to the different stages The Hero’s Journey is divided into:

The Ordinary World

The Call to Adventure

Refusal of the Call

Meeting with the Mentor

Crossing the Threshold to the Special World

Tests, Allies and Enemies

Approach to the Innermost Cave

The Ordeal

The Reward

The Road Back

The Resurrection

Return with the Elixir

 

All of these stages are divided into the three parts I mentioned above. The first part, the Departure, include the following stages:

The Ordinary World

The Call to Adventure

Refusal of the Call

Meeting with the Mentor

Crossing the Threshold to the Special World

 

The second part, the Initiation, include the following stages:

Tests, Allies and Enemies

Approach to the Innermost Cave

The Ordeal

The Reward

 

The third part, the Return, include the following stages:

The Road Back

The Resurrection

Return with the Elixir

 

Now, let’s dive deeper into these different stages of The Hero’s Journey.

 

THE ORDINARY WORLD
The Hero is introduced. He is shown in his Ordinary World, which is nothing special and a complete contrast to the Special World he will later venture into. He has a sad, boring life that usually gets the reader to sympathize and/or identify with him.

 

THE CALL TO ADVENTURE
Within his Ordinary World, the Hero receives some form of information that shakes up the situation and acts as the call to adventure. The Hero is being prompted to leave the Ordinary World for the Special World. This is where he is beginning a new stage in his life.

 

REFUSAL OF THE CALL
The Hero experience some refusal to answer the call and turn away from the adventure, perhaps by feelings of insecurity, obligation, or fear of the unknown.

 

MEETING WITH THE MENTOR
The Hero meets a guide or protector or some form of magical helper—often a seasoned traveler—who offer the Hero training, knowledge, confidence, advice, and such that will help the Hero on his journey. The key word is that the Mentor offers help and guidance while the Hero is the one who should complete the journey.

 

CROSSING THE THRESHOLD TO THE SPECIAL WORLD
At the end of this first part, the Departure, the Hero commits to leaving the Ordinary World and crossing into the adventure and the Special World. This new unknown and dangerous world contains rules the Hero is not familiar with. While the Mentor lead the Hero to the threshold, the Hero has to cross it on his own. The threshold is also guarded by a Guardian or Gatekeeper, which means the Hero must prove to be worthy in order to pass the threshold.

 

TESTS, ALLIES AND ENEMIES
The Hero explores this new and unknown world and goes through tests and trials within this unfamiliar setting. He learns new things and skills that will prepare him for the Ordeal that’s to come. The Hero should not succeed at every test, he should know what failure feels like (because this will make him grow). He will also encounter new characters and sort out friends from foes. His new companions will help him with the tests and trials.

 

APPROACH TO THE INNERMOST CAVE
The Hero prepares for the major challenge in the Special World—together with his friends—by facing greater challenges and more difficult obstacles and guardians. This is a way to prove himself worthy of greater challenges and the ultimate battle.

 

THE ORDEAL
The Hero faces his greatest challenge yet, in the form of the Antagonist, with the knowledge and skills he has obtained up until now. He confronts death or his deepest fear. He then experiences death and rebirth (either literal or symbolic).

 

THE REWARD
The Hero takes possession of the reward/treasure he won by facing his greatest challenge, marking his triumph over the Antagonist. This reward/treasure is what the Hero went on the journey to get (it does not have to be something material, though).

 

THE ROAD BACK
The Hero is driven to complete the adventure by going back to the Ordinary World with the reward/treasure he won. It can often be as dangerous to return from the journey as it was to start it in the first place. There is often a chase scene that signals the urgency and danger of the mission, or the defeated Antagonist may be rallying for a second round.

 

THE RESURRECTION
The Hero is once again tested on the threshold going back to the Ordinary World (this may be brought about by a rebounding Antagonist who must be conquered once more). The Hero experiences a final moment of death and resurrection that’s on a higher and more complete level than the previous one, so that he is pure when he reenters the Ordinary World. This resurrection may either be literal or symbolical, and he wakes to a new world and transformed life.

 

RETURN WITH THE ELIXIR
The Hero returns home with some element of the reward/treasure that will help him improve the Ordinary World (it can just as well be a material thing as a greater insight into himself as a person). Usually, the elixir (the reward/treasure) is meant to help someone other than the Hero—what the Hero gained on his journey will benefit others beyond himself.

 

There you have the Hero’s Journey in its simplest form. I hope this post has been useful.

Have you structured your story with The Hero’s Journey as a framework? If not, would you consider using it? Please do share in the comments below.

Departure

Return

Tests, Allies and Enemies

The Ordeal

The Reward

The Road Back

The Resurrection

The Hero is once again tested on the threshold going back to the Ordinary World (this may be brought about by a rebounding Antagonist who must be conquered once more). The Hero experiences a final moment of death and resurrection that’s on a higher and more complete level than the previous one, so that he is pure when he reenters the Ordinary World. This resurrection may either be literal or symbolical, and he wakes to a new world and transformed life.

 

RETURN WITH THE ELIXIR
The Hero returns home with some element of the reward/treasure that will help him improve the Ordinary World (it can just as well be a material thing as a greater insight into himself as a person). Usually, the elixir (the reward/treasure) is meant to help someone other than the Hero—what the Hero gained on his journey will benefit others beyond himself.

 

There you have the Hero’s Journey in its simplest form. I hope this post has been useful.
